speakers: Winston T. H. Koh (Singapore Management University)
summary: Do yield curve trades that bet on mean reversion of level, slope and curvature to the historical-average ('unconditional') curve earn excess payoffs? Method: cash-neutral, duration-weighted one-month trades on the Fama-Bliss zero curve 1973-2000, volatility-matched against a Lehman intermediate Treasury index and a cash-neutral S&P benchmark. Spread (2-B) and curvature (3-B) trades on adjacent maturities beat both benchmarks gross and, for 2-B, after costs, add alpha to an S&P holding, but the edge faded after the mid-1980s.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: that are based on the view that the yield curve mean-reverts to an unconditional curve.
claims.claim: The paper tests relative-value trades that bet the yield curve reverts to an unconditional (historical average) curve.
claims.exact_rule: Compare one-month forward curve with expanding-window average curve; trade toward the average.
claims.indicator: deviation of one-month forward curve from unconditional curve

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: These mean-reverting trading strategies exploit deviations in the level, slope and curvature of the yield curve from historical norms. We consider cash-neutral trades with one-month holding periods.
claims.claim: Three deviation types (level, slope, curvature) are traded with cash-neutral positions held one month.
claims.exact_rule: Level, slope, curvature deviations; cash neutral; 1-month holding period, rebalanced monthly.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: outperform, on a risk-adjusted basis before transaction costs, alternative strategies of an investment in the Lehman Brothers Bond index (by up to 5.9 times) and an investment in the S&P index (by up to 5.1 times)
claims.claim: Best mean-reverting strategies earn up to 5.9x the Lehman bond index and 5.1x the S&P benchmark on volatility-matched gross average payoff.
claims.reported_result: up to 5.9x Lehman Brothers index and 5.1x S&P, gross, volatility-matched (abstract; detail in Table 1)

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Even after accounting for transaction costs, some of these strategies are still significantly more profitable than the benchmarks.
claims.claim: After costs, only some strategies (2-B clearly) stay significantly better than the benchmarks.
claims.reported_result: see Table 3: 2-B significant on all tests, 3-B only on t-tests

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: transaction costs can be reduced substantially by changing the trading frequency or through structured derivative trades.
claims.claim: Costs can be cut by trading less often or using notional derivative structures.
claims.exact_rule: Lower rebalancing frequency (e.g. quarterly) or threshold-triggered entry; or swap/futures replication.
claims.testable: no - not tested in this paper

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: We found evidence that market efficiency has improved, and the scope for excess returns has diminished since the late 1980s.
claims.claim: The excess payoff of the strategies has shrunk since the late 1980s, which the authors attribute to improved market efficiency.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Relative-value trading, by contrast, focuses on the market view that the unconditional yield curve is upward sloping, and that the current yield curve would mean-revert to an unconditional yield curve.
claims.claim: Relative-value yield curve trading rests on the practitioner belief that the curve reverts to an upward-sloping unconditional curve.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Directional trading, as the name implies, are bets on changes in the interest rates in specific directions.
claims.claim: The paper separates directional trades (bets on rate direction) from relative-value trades, and studies only the latter.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: We consciously avoid “data-snooping” by not searching through a large number of possible strategies to find a few that are profitable.
claims.claim: To limit data snooping the authors derive a small, natural set of strategies from the single mean-reversion view rather than searching many.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: if the level, spread or curvature is higher (lower) than the historical average, bet that the level, spread or curvature, respectively, will decrease
claims.claim: Core rule: when level, spread or curvature is above its historical average, bet it falls (and vice versa).
claims.exact_rule: sign(deviation of level/slope/curvature from historical average) -> bet on reversal toward average
claims.indicator: level, spread, curvature vs historical average
claims.direction: long duration/steepener/butterfly when below average per class definition

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Litterman and Scheinkman (1991), Mann and Ramanlal (1997) and Drakos (2001) are recent studies on the subject.
claims.claim: Prior studies of yield curve trading performance cited: Litterman-Scheinkman, Mann-Ramanlal, Drakos.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Following Litterman and Scheinkman (1991), we consider the three aspects of the yield curve – namely, the interest rate level, the slope (i.e. yield spread) and the curvature
claims.claim: Level, slope and curvature follow Litterman-Scheinkman three-factor decomposition of curve moves.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: we impose cash neutrality and consider one-month holding period for each category of strategies, and adjust the payoff for risk, as measured by the standard deviation of the payoffs.
claims.claim: All strategies are cash-neutral, held one month, and compared after scaling to equal payoff standard deviation.
claims.exact_rule: cash neutral; 1-month hold; risk adjustment = scale to common payoff standard deviation

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Our study abstract from credit risk --in particular, default risk –
claims.claim: Study uses U.S. Treasuries only and ignores credit risk.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: from the period 1964 to 2000 for our study.
claims.claim: Sample period is 1964-2000 for data; payoffs measured from January 1973 to December 2000 (see C11).

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: This involves essentially buying fixed income assets and selling them before maturity to earn the term risk premium.
claims.claim: Benchmark 1 'riding the yield curve' earns the term risk premium by buying bonds and selling before maturity.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: some yield curve strategies outperform the S&P strategy by about 5.1 times, and the Lehman Brothers Bond index strategy about 5.9 times, based on a comparison of the risk-adjusted average gross payoffs.
claims.claim: Headline multiples: best strategy about 5.1x S&P and 5.9x Lehman index on risk-adjusted average gross payoff.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: the implied transaction costs that would have eliminated the excess returns from the set profitable mean-reverting yield curve trades is of the order of about 0.01% of the value of bonds traded
claims.claim: Breakeven transaction cost that wipes out the excess return is about 0.01% of bonds traded.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: than the current transaction cost in the market for U.S. Treasury bills (but not Treasury bonds).
claims.claim: The breakeven cost is below the then-current Treasury bill cost but above Treasury bond cost, so physical bill trading would not clear it.
claims.conditions: costs of bills vs bonds in 2003-04
claims.testable: partly - cost data not given here

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: the implied transaction cost we calculated is based on the assumption of entering and exiting each yield curve trading strategy on a monthly basis.
claims.claim: Breakeven cost assumes full monthly entry and exit, i.e. maximum turnover.
claims.exact_rule: full monthly turnover of all legs

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: The transaction costs can be significantly reduced by structuring derivative trades on a notional basis, mirroring the economic cashflows of the underlying yield curve trades but without actually funding and holding the bonds.
claims.claim: Replicating the trades with notional derivatives avoids funding and holding bonds and cuts costs.
claims.exact_rule: derivative (swap/futures) replication of the same cash flows

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: There is a wide variety of yield curve trading strategies.
claims.claim: Yield-curve trading literature is old (from the late 1960s) and broad; authors cite De Leonardis, Freund, Darst, Weberman, Dyl-Joehnk, Stigum-Fabozzi.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: This market view is consistent with historical experience. For instance, U.S. Treasury bill rates, spreads and curvature all trade within tight, finite bounds.
claims.claim: Mean reversion is supported by observation that bill rates, spreads and curvature stay in finite bounds, and other countries show the same.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: This suggests that some form of mean-reversion mechanism is at work that prevents the yield curve from drifting to extreme levels or shapes over time.
claims.claim: Bounded yield curve behaviour is read as evidence of a mean-reverting mechanism; none is identified.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: The market view of yield curve mean-reversion is also represented in theoretical models of the interest rate term structure – as discussed in Vasicek (1977), Cox, Ingersoll and Ross (1981, 1985), and Campbell and Shiller (1991)
claims.claim: Vasicek, CIR and Campbell-Shiller term structure models embed mean reversion.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: the pure expectations hypothesis of the term structure is the theory that the long-term interest rate is the average of the current and expected short-term rates, so that the yield spread is mean-reverting.
claims.claim: Pure expectations hypothesis: long rate = average of expected short rates, so the spread is mean-reverting.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: the pure expectations hypothesis implies that excess returns on long bonds over short bonds are unforecastable, with a zero mean in the case of the pure expectations hypothesis.
claims.claim: Under rational expectations plus the pure EH, bond excess returns are unforecastable with zero mean, so no strategy should pay consistently.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: pure expectations hypothesis, yield curve trading strategies attempting to exploit anomalies or mis-pricings in the term structure would not yield consistently positive payoffs.
claims.claim: Pure EH therefore predicts mean-reverting curve trades earn nothing; positive payoffs would reject it.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: It is easy to see that bullet strategies are essentially bets on the level of the interest rates, while ladder strategies and barbell strategies are bets on the yield spreads and curvatures, respectively.
claims.claim: Practitioner bullet, ladder, barbell structures map to level, slope, curvature bets.
claims.exact_rule: bullet=level; ladder=slope; barbell=curvature

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: He found that the holding period returns were very different from observed spot interest rates, and concluded that the pure expectations hypothesis, as propounded by Lutz (1940)
claims.claim: Culbertson (1957) found one-to-three-week holding period returns very different from spot rates and rejected the pure EH.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Shiller, Campbell and Schoenholtz (1983) showed that the term structure does not provide information on the future change in the
claims.claim: Shiller-Campbell-Schoenholtz (1983): the term structure carries no information on future short-rate changes.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Mankiw and Miron (1986) also found that the predictability of the term structure disappears after the founding of the Federal Reserve.
claims.claim: Mankiw-Miron (1986): term-structure predictability disappears after the Fed was founded.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Rudebusch (1995) and Balduzzi, Bertola and Foresi (1997) also found that changes in the interest rate were due to unexpected changes in the Fed targeting.
claims.claim: Rudebusch and Balduzzi-Bertola-Foresi: rate changes are driven by unexpected Fed target changes.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: The dataset we use for our study is the Fama-Bliss dataset obtained from CRSP
claims.claim: Data: CRSP Fama-Bliss zero-coupon yields derived from US Treasury bills and bonds.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: The data set contains monthly data on zero coupon yields derived from a yield curve of U.S. government Treasury bills and bonds from 30 June 1964 to 29 December 2000.
claims.claim: Sample spans 30 June 1964 to 29 December 2000 with 439 monthly curves.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: we express all zero coupon yields in the form of continuously compounded yields. These zero-coupon yields are of maturities that are approximately 1-month, 2-month,…, 12-
claims.claim: Yields are continuously compounded, at about 1..12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 months maturity.
claims.exact_rule: continuously compounded zero yields; observed tenors 1-12,24,36,48,60 months

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: First, we perform a cross-sectional linear interpolation to each zero yield curve in order to obtain the yields at monthly tenors from 1-month to 60-month.
claims.claim: Step 1: linearly interpolate each curve across maturity to get every monthly tenor 1-60.
claims.exact_rule: cross-sectional linear interpolation of zero yields to 1..60 month tenors

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Hypothetical bonds therefore have maturities greater than 12 months, but are not divisible by 12.
claims.claim: Bonds at observed tenors are 'primary'; interpolated ones (maturity >12 months, not multiple of 12) are 'hypothetical'; results are shown for both.
claims.exact_rule: primary = observed tenors; hypothetical = interpolated tenors

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: The second step that we took to regularize the dataset is a temporal linear interpolation procedure.
claims.claim: Step 2: observation dates are linearly interpolated in time so curves are exactly one month apart.
claims.exact_rule: temporal linear interpolation of each tenor's yield to a grid of 30.4375 days

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: we define this to be 365.25 days divided by 12, i.e. 30.4375 days.
claims.claim: One month is defined as 30.4375 days.
claims.exact_rule: month length = 365.25/12 = 30.4375 days

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Since the holding period of each trade is one-month, the relevant forward yield curve with which to compare against the unconditional yield curve is the one-month forward yield curve.
claims.claim: The signal compares the one-month forward curve (not spot) with the unconditional curve.
claims.exact_rule: signal curve = 1-month-ahead forward yield curve

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: The one-month forward interest rate at a maturity of X months is calculated as follows.
claims.exact_rule: r_{x,1} = ((x+1)*r_{x+1,0} - r_{1,0})/x using continuously compounded yields (equation read from page 10 image)

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: the unconditional yield at each maturity (for primary and hypothetical bonds) at any date is calculated as the simple average of all the yields observed for that maturity since June 1964 till the preceding month.
claims.claim: Unconditional curve = expanding-window simple average of each maturity's yield since June 1964, excluding the current month.
claims.exact_rule: U_x(t) = mean over s from Jun-1964 to t-1 of yield_x(s); expanding window, no look-ahead

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Figure 1 below illustrates the unconditional yield curve for various dates.
claims.claim: The unconditional curve is upward sloping and concave, rises over time as new high-rate data enter (Dec-1972 ~4.6% at 1m to 5.6% at 60m; Dec-1986 peak ~6.8% to 7.9%; Dec-2000 ~6.2% to 7.4%).

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: For each strategy, the holding period of a trade is fixed at one month, after which a new trade is initiated. We impose the condition of cash neutrality, so that any excess cash is deposited at the 1-month tenor.
claims.claim: Trades rebalance monthly; any cash surplus is deposited and any shortfall borrowed at the 1-month tenor.
claims.exact_rule: monthly full re-initiation; residual cash at 1-month rate

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: As a bond of maturity X months has a duration of ( X − 1) months, the deposits and borrowings at the one-month tenor have no impact on the duration of each trade.
claims.claim: A zero-coupon bond of X months has duration X-1 months after one month; 1-month cash has zero duration, so funding does not alter duration.
claims.exact_rule: duration after one month = X-1 months

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: We allow for a 102-month training period in the construction of the unconditional yield curve, so that our calculation of the average payoff of each yield-
claims.claim: 102-month training period; payoffs measured January 1973 to December 2000.
claims.exact_rule: burn-in 102 months (Jul-1964 to Dec-1972); evaluation Jan-1973 to Dec-2000

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: A reason for the selection of the training period is the fact that the Lehman Brothers U.S. Government Intermediate Bond Index starts in January 1973.
claims.claim: Start date is dictated by availability of the Lehman Intermediate Government index (Jan 1973).
claims.data_needed: Lehman Brothers US Government Intermediate Bond Index from Jan 1973

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: This strategy takes the view that the average level of the yield curve mean- reverts to that of the unconditional yield curve.
claims.claim: Strategy 1-A: compare the average level of the forward curve with the average of the unconditional curve.
claims.exact_rule: signal = mean over maturities of 1m-forward yields minus mean of unconditional yields

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: The implied strategy is to go long (short) all the bonds with maturities longer than one month.
claims.claim: 1-A: forward level above average -> long all bonds >1 month; below -> short them.
claims.exact_rule: if avg forward > avg unconditional: long all bonds maturity>1m; else short; fund/deposit at 1m
claims.direction: long duration when level above historical average

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: the amount of cash invested in a bond of maturity of X months, with duration of ( X − 1) months, will be k /( X − 1) dollar.
claims.claim: 1-A sizing: invest k/(X-1) dollars in each X-month bond so each contributes equally to a parallel shift (k/59 in the 60-month bond).
claims.exact_rule: weight_X = k/(X-1) per bond, funds borrowed or deposited at 1-month

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: In this strategy, a parallel shift in the yield curve generates approximately equal contribution to the payoff at each maturity.
claims.claim: Duration weighting equalises each maturity's contribution to a parallel shift payoff.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: If the one-month forward yield is higher (lower) than the corresponding level on the unconditional yield curve, the expectation is that one- month forward yield curve would fall (rise).
claims.claim: 1-B: signal per maturity; yield above its unconditional level -> expect fall.
claims.exact_rule: for each X>=2: sign(forward_X - unconditional_X) determines long (above) or short (below) the X-month bond, size k/(X-1), 1-month leg funds
claims.indicator: yield at each maturity vs unconditional

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: We consider two versions of the trade, one for maturities of only primary bonds, and another for maturities, including all the interpolated maturities of the hypothetical bonds.
claims.claim: 1-B is run on primary-only and on all (primary + hypothetical) maturities.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: The implied strategy is to go long (short) the 60-month bond and go short (long) the 2-month bond.
claims.claim: 2-A: if 59m-1m forward spread is above average, long the 60-month and short the 2-month bond (slope falls); reverse otherwise.
claims.exact_rule: spread = fwd(59m)-fwd(1m) vs unconditional; spread high: long 60m bond (k/59) short 2m bond (k); low: reverse
claims.direction: long long-end bond vs short-end when spread above average (as the paper states)

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Suppose k /59 dollars are invested in the 60- month bond, we need to short the 2-month bond by k dollars, to achieve duration- matching. The excess cash of 58 k /59 dollars is deposited in the one-month tenor.
claims.claim: 2-A sizing: k/59 in 60-month, short k in 2-month, 58k/59 cash at 1-month; duration neutral and cash neutral.
claims.exact_rule: long k/59 of 60m; short k of 2m; deposit 58k/59 at 1m; zero net duration

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: A parallel shift in the yield curve has negligible impact on the payoff.
claims.claim: 2-A is immune to parallel shifts by construction.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: the yield spread between two adjacent bonds of maturities ( X −1) months and ( Y −1) months, with Y > X , on the one-month forward yield curve would mean-revert to the corresponding spread on the unconditional yield curve.
claims.claim: 2-B: apply the mean-reverting spread view separately to each pair of adjacent bonds on the forward curve.
claims.exact_rule: for each adjacent pair (X,Y): spread_forward vs spread_unconditional

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: forward spread is larger (smaller) than that for the unconditional curve, go long the bond, with maturity of Y months, and short the bond with maturity of X months.
claims.claim: 2-B rule: spread above average -> long the Y (longer) bond and short the X bond; below -> reverse.
claims.exact_rule: if spread(Y,X) fwd > unconditional: long Y short X; else long X short Y
claims.direction: long longer bond vs shorter bond when spread above average

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: We duration- weight each leg of the trade so that changes in the yield spread with equal magnitude across different trades would generate approximately equal payoff contribution to the portfolio.
claims.claim: 2-B legs are duration-weighted (cash k/(Z-1) per leg) so equal spread changes across pairs give equal payoff.
claims.exact_rule: cash per leg = k/(Z-1); legs sum across all pairs; cash-neutral via 1m deposit/borrow

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: We consider two versions of the trade, for both yield curves with only primary bonds and another set with maturities one month apart from one month to 60 months.
claims.claim: 2-B is run with primary bonds only (observed tenors, 14 segments) and with all monthly maturities.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: The curvature of the curve yield curve, as defined by the three bonds, is the measure:
claims.claim: Curvature of three maturities X<Y<Z (Eq. 2): c(X,Y,Z) = (r_Y - r_X)/(Y - X) - (r_Z - r_Y)/(Z - Y), using one-month forward yields.
claims.exact_rule: c(X,Y,Z)=(r_Y-r_X)/(Y-X) - (r_Z-r_Y)/(Z-Y) (equation read from page 14 image)

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: If the curvature is smaller (larger) relative to the corresponding measure for the unconditional yield curve over the same set of maturities, the expectation is that the curvature of the one-month forward yield curve would increase (decrease).
claims.claim: Curvature signal: forward curvature below the unconditional value -> expect increase.
claims.exact_rule: sign(c_unconditional - c_forward) over the same X,Y,Z

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: we consider the maturities of 1-month, 29-month (a hypothetical bond, and the mid-point) and the 59- month bond, on the one-month forward yield curve.
claims.claim: 3-A uses three points (1m, 29m, 59m forward) for a whole-curve curvature measure.
claims.exact_rule: c(1,29,59) on 1m forward curve vs same on unconditional curve

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: bond and short (long) the 30-month bond, on the current yield curve. We match the durations of the various portions of the trade as follows.
claims.claim: 3-A direction: expect curvature to rise -> long 2m and 60m, short 30m (barbell); expect fall -> reverse.
claims.exact_rule: curvature low: long 2m, long 60m, short 30m; high: reverse (bonds are those with durations 1, 29, 59 on the 1m forward curve)
claims.direction: long wings short belly when curvature below average

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: for the 30-month bond (with a duration of 29 months), the amount to short is 2 k /29 dollars.
claims.claim: 3-A sizing: k/59 in 60m, k in 2m, short 2k/29 in 30m; borrowing covers the net funding need; duration zero.
claims.exact_rule: long k/59 (60m); long k (2m); short 2k/29 (30m); borrow remainder at 1m; net duration zero (paper's funding expression is typographically garbled)
claims.testable: partly - funding formula garbled in text

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: The trade is cash-neutral and has zero duration, so that a parallel shift in the yield curve or a change in the slope of the yield curve without a change in curvature has negligible impacts on the payoff.
claims.claim: 3-A is immune to level and slope shifts by construction, so it isolates curvature.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: we compare the curvature of any three adjacent bonds, say with maturities of ( X− 1), ( Y− 1) and ( Z− 1) months on the 1-month forward yield curve
claims.claim: 3-B: every triplet of adjacent primary bonds is its own curvature trade vs the unconditional curvature.
claims.exact_rule: for each adjacent triplet (X,Y,Z): c_forward vs c_unconditional; if smaller: long X and Z, short Y; if larger: reverse
claims.direction: long wings short belly when curvature below average

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: the cash amount is given by 2 k /( Y − 1) dollars.
claims.claim: 3-B sizing: k/(X-1) and k/(Z-1) in the wings, 2k/(Y-1) in the belly; funding = k/(X-1)+k/(Z-1)-2k/(Y-1).
claims.exact_rule: wings k/(X-1), k/(Z-1); belly 2k/(Y-1); residual at 1m

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: The strategy is essentially a portfolio of curvature trades, using all the primary bonds.
claims.claim: 3-B portfolio sums all adjacent-triplet curvature trades over primary bonds.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Since the hypothetical bonds are linearly interpolated from the primary bonds, the curvatures of the hypothetical bonds are zero. Hence, the trade does not work with hypothetical bonds.
claims.claim: 3-B can only use primary bonds because interpolated bonds have zero curvature by construction.

claims.speaker: Chua, Koh, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: This benchmark is constructed by assuming that we go long on the Lehman Brothers U.S. Government Intermediate Bond Index. The trade is funded by shorting 1- month Treasury bills.
claims.claim: Benchmark 1: long Lehman Intermediate Government index, short 1-month T-bills, cash-neutral.
claims.exact_rule: Benchmark1 payoff = Lehman intermediate index return - 1m T-bill return
claims.data_needed: Lehman Brothers US Govt Intermediate Index; 1m T-bill

reasoning.question: Can a systematic trader earn reliable, risk-adjusted profits by betting that the US Treasury curve's level, slope and curvature return to their long-run averages, against the expectations-hypothesis view that such curve trades cannot pay consistently, and do these profits survive costs and add value to an equity portfolio?

thesis.statement: Local mean-reversion trades on adjacent-maturity spreads (2-B) and curvature (3-B) of the one-month forward Treasury curve earned 3-6x the risk-adjusted payoff of bond and equity benchmarks in 1973-2000, with 2-B still significant after costs; level trades did not work, and the edge shrank markedly after the 1980s.

foundations.premise: The Treasury curve's level, slope and curvature are bounded and revert to a historical norm.
foundations.support: observation that rates, spreads and curvature stay in tight bounds here and abroad; mean-reverting term-structure models

foundations.premise: The expectations hypothesis (which would rule out consistent curve-trade profits) does not hold empirically.
foundations.support: citations: Culbertson 1957, Hamburger-Platt 1975, Shiller-Campbell-Schoenholtz 1983, Mankiw-Miron 1986, CIR 1985

foundations.premise: Maturity segments are partly segmented by preferred habitats/ALM constraints, so cross-sector arbitrage is incomplete.
foundations.support: intuition plus the location of the most profitable trade segments (offered after the results)

foundations.premise: The expanding full-history average since 1964 is the right anchor ('unconditional curve') for each maturity.
foundations.support: none beyond the mean-reversion premise; no alternative anchors tested

foundations.premise: Comparing strategies at equal payoff volatility is a fair way to rank fixed income and equity strategies.
foundations.support: argued as addressing comparability of risk, holding period and credit

mechanism_chain.from: Local spread/curvature of the forward curve deviates from its long-run norm
mechanism_chain.to: Deviation is not arbitraged away quickly because investors stay in preferred maturity habitats (especially around the 12-month short/long-end boundary)
mechanism_chain.why: ALM constraints restrict lenders/borrowers to sectors so they do not shift to exploit forward vs expected rate gaps

mechanism_chain.to: Over the next month the forward-curve feature moves back toward the norm
mechanism_chain.why: some mean-reversion mechanism keeps the curve within bounds

mechanism_chain.from: Duration-weighted, cash-neutral position on the deviation
mechanism_chain.to: Profit roughly proportional to the size of the deviation, insulated from parallel (and for curvature, slope) moves
mechanism_chain.why: equal dollar-duration legs isolate the targeted feature

mechanism_chain.from: Better information, liquidity, computing and telecoms
mechanism_chain.to: Faster arbitrage, shrinking excess returns since the mid/late 1980s
mechanism_chain.why: traders can rapidly seek out these opportunities

design_rationale.choice: Trade only strategies directly implied by mean reversion (6 strategies) rather than search
Signal on the one-month forward curve vs expanding-mean unconditional curve
design_rationale.reason_given: holding period is one month, so the forward curve is the right comparison
design_rationale.alternatives: not compared with spot-curve signals or rolling windows

design_rationale.choice: Binary sign of deviation sets direction; size fixed (k), not scaled by deviation
design_rationale.alternatives: threshold trading mentioned as a cost-saving idea
design_rationale.sensitivity: not shown, though Figures 7-8 imply deviation-proportional sizing would matter

design_rationale.choice: Duration weighting k/(X-1) per leg and cash at 1-month tenor
design_rationale.reason_given: equal payoff contribution per unit move; isolate level/slope/curvature; 1-month cash adds no duration

design_rationale.choice: Adjacent-segment portfolios (2-B, 3-B) vs single whole-curve trades (2-A, 3-A)
design_rationale.reason_given: consider whole curve and individual portions
design_rationale.sensitivity: local versions far better: 2-B 5.7x vs 2-A 0.37x bond benchmark

design_rationale.reason_given: compare structures; curvature on interpolated points is zero
design_rationale.sensitivity: 2-B nearly identical; level strategies worse with H

design_rationale.reason_given: fair comparison; decisions remain out of sample

design_rationale.choice: Cost model: half of 1bp yield spread times maturity, benchmarks cost-free
design_rationale.reason_given: Bloomberg spreads ~1bp or less; half-spread per trade
design_rationale.alternatives: quarterly/threshold trading and derivatives mentioned but not tested

evidence_map.result: 2-B and 3-B beat both benchmarks at equal volatility (2-B ~5x, 3-B ~3.3-3.8x) before costs
evidence_map.tests: mean reversion of local spreads/curvature is exploitable (step 2)
evidence_map.rules_out: pure expectations hypothesis zero-mean excess returns for these trades in 1973-2000
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) compensation for a risk not captured by S&P/Lehman benchmarks (e.g. liquidity or crash risk in short-end segments); artefacts of Fama-Bliss bill interpolation at 1-12 months; full-sample vol scaling
evidence_map.strength: strong - t up to 11.8, DM p 0.001 for 2-B

evidence_map.result: Level reversion (1-A, 1-B) and whole-curve slope (2-A) fail; whole-curve curvature (3-A) not significant
evidence_map.tests: which aspect reverts at a 1-month horizon
evidence_map.rules_out: simple level mean-reversion as a source of profit
evidence_map.strength: moderate - point estimates only for level strategies

evidence_map.result: 2-B remains significant net of costs (DM p 0.0102/0.0135); 3-B only on t-tests
evidence_map.rules_out: that 2-B gains are purely a cost illusion at 0.5bp half-spread
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) higher realised costs for 1-2 month bills or market impact; historical spreads in the 1970s-80s far wider than the 2003 Bloomberg numbers used
evidence_map.strength: moderate - cost assumption from 2003 applied to 1973-2000

evidence_map.tests: step 3: profit scales with mispricing size
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) mechanical relation from interpolation/measurement noise in the data (noise in one month's curve reverses next month); the chosen triple differs between text and figure

evidence_map.tests: diversification value for an equity investor
evidence_map.rules_out: that the gains are S&P beta
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) exposure to bond-market factors (term premium) not in the regression

evidence_map.result: 10-year moving averages shrink; 3-B falls below benchmarks
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) changes in rate volatility regime (high 1979-82 volatility inflates early deviations), changes in Fama-Bliss data quality, Fed policy regime

evidence_map.result: Profit concentrated at the very short end (1-3 month) and at 10-11/10-11-23 months
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) the 12-month boundary is also where Fama-Bliss switches from bill data to interpolated 24-month point, so it may be a data artefact

regimes.effect: 3-B below benchmarks; 2-B lower but still above benchmarks

regimes.condition: Large absolute deviations from the norm
Transaction cost above ~0.01% of value traded (e.g. bills)

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Figure 8 shows the 9-10-11 month curvature trade while the text says the 10-11-23 triple was plotted
Text dates the 3-B decline from ~1984 and below benchmarks by 1990, but Figure 10 (window-end dating) shows the peak in 1988 and crossing near 1993-94
Authors call autocorrelations small and mixed, but Figures 2-3 show mostly positive autocorrelations of 0.1-0.36 at short lags, which inflate paired t-stats
Table 3 note says it lists breakeven costs, but it shows net payoffs and tests; the 0.01% breakeven figure is not shown in any table
Text says 2-B is 5.1x/5.9x (H version, $29.51) while Table 2 tests the P version (4.96x/5.68x)
3-A funding formula printed as k(1/59 + 1 - 2k/29); dimensionally should be k(1/59 + 1 - 2/29)
Bonferroni counts 6 strategies though 8 variants (P/H) and 3 comparisons per strategy were tested; 3-B DM p-values (0.0158/0.0258) fail the 0.00833 threshold
Volatility scaling uses full-sample standard deviations (look-ahead in position size); no rolling-vol version
2003 bid-ask spreads applied to 1973-2000; earlier spreads were much wider; no market impact or financing (repo) costs
Interpolated 1-12 month Fama-Bliss bill yields and linear interpolation between 12 and 24 months may create artificial local spreads/curvature that mean-revert mechanically
Pair count for 2-B primary version: Figure 5 lists 14 forward-curve pairs (1-2 .. 47-59); exact mapping of forward maturities to traded bonds is only implied
3-B legs (k, 2k, k over durations) are neutral to parallel shifts but not to slope when maturities are unequally spaced (e.g. 10-11-23)
Whether Foster-Stine regressions (Table 4) and Figures 7-8 ('net profit') use gross or net payoffs is not fully explicit
Segmentation explanation offered after the fact; no test of holder habitats

reasoning.forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Adjacent-maturity forward spreads and three-point curvatures on the 1-month forward Treasury curve, measured against their long-run (expanding) means, predict the next month's change in those spreads/curvatures (step 2 of the chain); the larger the gap the larger the expected move. The signal works through slow cross-sector arbitrage between short-end (bill) and longer note habitats. It stops working when arbitrage capital, liquidity and technology close gaps quickly (as seen after the late 1980s), when trading costs exceed ~0.01% of value traded, or when curve 'deviations' are mostly data noise. Level deviations do not predict at one month.
reader_inferences: (reader) Ratios of mean payoffs at equal volatility are ratios of Sharpe ratios, so 2-B's Sharpe ratio is about 5x the S&P excess-return Sharpe ratio over 1973-2000.
(reader) Costs absorbed about 20% of 2-B's gross mean payoff (0.02851 -> 0.02267) and about 36% of 3-B's (0.01917 -> 0.01234).
(reader) Positive short-lag autocorrelations in Figures 2-3 mean paired t-statistics overstate significance; the DM results are the ones to rely on.
(reader) The 0.814/0.763 correlations equal sqrt of the R-squares printed on Figures 7-8 (0.66242, 0.58186).
(reader) Much of 2-B's profit comes from the 1-3 month bill spreads, where bill yields are noisiest and costs highest relative to duration, so live replication may capture less.
(reader) The 12-month concentration coincides with the boundary between observed bill maturities and the 24-month point in Fama-Bliss data, so part of the edge may be interpolation-driven.
(reader) Inconsistencies between text and figures (Figure 8 triple, Figure 10 dating) suggest the text was written for an earlier version of the exhibits.
(reader) The strategies are contrarian to curve moves; they complement trend-following and carry signals in a macro book but on the short end are likely to have capacity limits.
(reader) Deviation-proportional sizing, rather than the paper's fixed-size sign bets, is a natural improvement suggested by Figures 7-8.
